messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Koa is a 42-year-old electrician who lives with his partner in a quiet suburb. He grew up in a large extended family on an island in the Pacific before moving to the mainland for work, and he still speaks with the soft, careful cadence of someone who learned English as a second language. He came to see me about six months after the assault, though he told me it took him that long to admit he needed to.

The event happened on a late autumn afternoon, around four o'clock. Koa was working alone in the basement of an old commercial building, running conduit along a ceiling joist. He had his back to the door. He heard it swing open and slam against the wall, and before he could turn around, a hand seized his shoulder and spun him. He remembers a face — the man was a former coworker who had been fired weeks earlier, drunk, shouting about something Koa had said to the foreman. What Koa remembers most vividly is not the punch that broke his jaw, but the moments just before: the sound of the door, the grip on his shoulder, the fraction of a second when his mind went blank and his body did not move. He remembers that blankness as a kind of failure. He told me he has tried to replay the sequence a thousand times, but it never connects properly. There is the door slamming, and then there is the man's face, and then there is the pain — and between those snapshots there is nothing, a gap that makes him feel as though he must have frozen, must have done something wrong, must have been the sort of person who just stands there while someone comes at him.

That interpretation has become the lens through which he sees everything now. He is certain that a different kind of man — someone tougher, someone more aware, someone worth protecting — would have heard the footsteps, would have turned in time, would not have been in that basement at that hour in the first place. He told me he has come to believe the event happened to him because of who he is fundamentally: someone passive, someone naive, someone who walks through the world with his guard down and therefore deserves whatever finds him. When he says this, his voice is flat, as though stating an obvious fact. He does not argue when I gently suggest otherwise; he simply waits for me to move on, and I understand that his conviction is not something he feels he needs to defend.

The immediate aftermath was functional in a narrow sense. Koa did not miss a day of work. He went back to the same job site the following week, though he refused to go into the basement. His foreman accommodated him, and over the following months the accommodations quietly multiplied. He stopped taking jobs in buildings he had never worked in before. He told his dispatcher he preferred commercial sites he already knew, and because he was a reliable and skilled electrician, no one pushed back. He stopped agreeing to work late shifts. He began leaving at three thirty every day, regardless of what was still unfinished, because by four o'clock he could feel something in his chest start to lock. He did not explain why. He simply stopped taking those calls.

At home, his partner noticed changes. Koa had always been a light drinker, but now he started having two or three beers every evening, and sometimes more on weekends. He told himself it was to unwind, but he knew on some level it was to dull the edge of the afternoon, to push the four o'clock hour past into the blur of evening without having to sit inside it. He also spent more and more time on his phone — scrolling through videos, playing simple puzzle games, anything that filled his attention and left no room for the snapshots to surface. His partner would ask if he wanted to watch a movie, and he would say no, because he had learned that any film with a scene of sudden violence — even a bar fight, even a shove — could send him into a state where his heart pounded and he felt as though the room was not real. He avoided TV news for the same reason. He told me he did not want to see anyone else get hurt, but what he meant, I think, was that he could not afford to have his own hurt re-lit.

His body stays on alert in ways that exhaust him. If someone approaches him from the side and touches his arm to get his attention, he flinches hard, sometimes enough that the other person pulls back apologetically. At work, he has learned to position himself so that no one can come up behind him. On the street, if another pedestrian steps suddenly into his peripheral vision, his shoulders jerk and his breath catches before he can tell his brain it is nothing. He avoids unfamiliar places entirely now — new restaurants, friends' houses he has not been to before, even a hardware store on the other side of town. He told me it is not that he expects to be attacked in those places. It is that he cannot assess the danger, cannot run the mental checklist of exits and sightlines and escape routes, and so he stays where he knows every corner.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment with his partner. He had been sitting on the couch in the late afternoon, phone in hand, beer on the table, when he realised he could not remember anything about the past three hours. He had scrolled through video after video, had drunk enough to feel numb, and the time had simply vanished. His partner sat down beside him and asked if he was okay, and Koa looked at her and thought about the future — or rather, he tried to think about the future and found nothing there, no image of himself a year from now, no plan, no desire, no point. It was not sadness, he told me. It was a kind of emptiness where a future should have been. He said he felt as though he was already gone, just waiting for his body to catch up. He agreed to come see me because he did not know what else to do, and because he could see in his partner's face that she was afraid for him. What he hopes, he told me quietly, is that someone can help him find the missing pieces of what happened, so that he might finally understand why he is the person this thing happened to. What he is most afraid of is that the answer is simply that he always was.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Auditory (Door): The vignette describes the door sound in the trauma narrative but does not show that hearing doors opening or slamming currently triggers a reaction.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
